rv.q: As for the devoted twins, the only strife that could truly affect them is sororal, and so the plot duly pulls them apart.
Wanted , as a modestly diverting entertainment, didn't need to make history, but its failure to spin a dizzying yarn out of an intriguing bit of family lore is a missed opportunity.
Add in a less-than-riveting performance from James, who has weak sauce to work with, and 'Wanted' ultimately falls off what initially looked like very promising rails.

In the end, because of its overstuffed book and themes, 'Wanted' doesn't quite know what it's about, resulting in an underwhelming account of who the Clarke sisters were and why their story stands out in American history.
This is a western that's not wild enough, a melodrama lacking heat, a song showcase that grows repetitive in all its smooth and unsurprising melody.
Wanted remains patchy in its serviceable-to-good lyricism, but it refreshingly paves a less trod path on the Great White Way.
Flawed as it may be, Wanted has a winning quality that constantly breaks through.
Wanted is giving Broadway something genuinely new and exciting. And yet, it never ascends to something bigger than the sum of its parts.
Too many of the two dozen musical numbers in 'Wanted' force the show's first-rate singers to start full-throttle and rarely dip into a more moderate register.

That leaves the very strong cast and the varied score to carry the day, which some may find to be enough. But for my money, there is a terrific story that gets lost among the little 'plotlets' and leaves Wanted wanting.

Neatly meshing effective performances and terrific singing with excellent visuals, Stevie Walker-Webb, the director, delivers Wanted as a solid Broadway production that looks as good as it sounds in Beowulf Boritt’s handsome scenic design.
And while it doesn't always hit the mark, there's still much to applaud.
What precedes it might be the dullest crime spree ever staged, with Walker-Webb's direction unable to find any real focus.
Wanted's overdramatic, self-serious script and under-dramatic score prevent the show from living up to its refreshingly audacious ambitions.
Ms. Chéri has used that creative license to craft a fable of oppression and empowerment that can seem both sanctimonious and silly.
Wanted is still worth the bounty.
For all its flaws, Wanted earns its place in the spotlight — and challenges us to consider why we still call the Midtown theater district the Great White Way.
Wanted is fast-paced, fabulous and absolutely worth fawning over. And I'm calling it now: It's going to be highly competitive come Tony season .
